cse-2025-2-cs-43.approach: Build the precedence graph of each schedule: an edge $T_i \to T_j$ for every conflicting pair (same item, different transactions, at least one write) where $T_i$'s operation comes first. A schedule is conflict serializable iff the graph is acyclic. With only two transactions, it is enough to check whether edges point both ways.
cse-2025-2-cs-43.given:
| T1 | T2 |
|---|---|
| R1(X), W1(Y), R1(X), W1(X) | W2(X), W2(Y) |

Conflicting pairs (different transactions, same item, at least one write): every T1 operation on X with W2(X), and W1(Y) with W2(Y). COMMITs never conflict.

steps.title: (A): R1(X) before W2(X), but W2(X) before the second R1(X)
steps.body:
(A) = R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), …

- first R1(X) then W2(X) (RW on X) ⇒ $T_1 \to T_2$
- W2(X) then the second R1(X) (WR on X) ⇒ $T_2 \to T_1$

Edges in both directions form a cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$ ⇒ **not** conflict serializable.

steps.title: (B): every conflict has T2 first
steps.body:
(B) = W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)

- W2(X) before both R1(X) and before W1(X) ⇒ $T_2 \to T_1$
- W2(Y) before W1(Y) ⇒ $T_2 \to T_1$

Only the edge $T_2 \to T_1$: acyclic ⇒ **conflict serializable**, equivalent to the serial order $T_2, T_1$.

scene.caption: (B): only T2 → T1 ⇒ equivalent to serial T2, T1

steps.title: (C): T1 first on Y, T2 first on the second read of X
steps.body:
(C) = R1(X), W1(Y), W2(X), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), …

- R1(X) before W2(X) ⇒ $T_1 \to T_2$; W1(Y) before W2(Y) ⇒ $T_1 \to T_2$
- W2(X) before the second R1(X) and W1(X) ⇒ $T_2 \to T_1$

Cycle ⇒ **not** conflict serializable.

steps.title: (D): T2 first on X, T1 first on Y
steps.body:
(D) = W2(X), R1(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), …

- W2(X) before R1(X) ⇒ $T_2 \to T_1$
- W1(Y) before W2(Y) ⇒ $T_1 \to T_2$

Cycle ⇒ **not** conflict serializable. Only (B) survives.

answer.value: Only schedule **(B)** is conflict serializable (equivalent to serial $T_2, T_1$)

optionAnalysis.reason: R1(X) precedes W2(X) ($T_1 \to T_2$) and W2(X) precedes the second R1(X) ($T_2 \to T_1$): cycle.
W2(X) and W2(Y) precede every conflicting T1 operation, so the only edge is $T_2 \to T_1$.
T1 is first on Y and on the first read of X, but W2(X) precedes the second R1(X) and W1(X): cycle.
T2 is first on X but W1(Y) precedes W2(Y): edges both ways. Note the COMMIT positions are irrelevant to conflict serializability.

cse-2025-2-cs-43.shortcut: With two transactions, look only at "who touches each item first". T2 must be first on both X and Y (it writes both), and T1 must not read or write X before W2(X). Only (B) starts with W2(X) and has W2(Y) before W1(Y).
pitfalls: Treating the two R1(X) operations as non-conflicting with W2(X) — a read conflicts with a write by another transaction.
Letting COMMIT positions decide; conflict serializability ignores commits (they matter for recoverability, not for the precedence graph).
Forgetting the WW conflict W1(Y)/W2(Y).
cse-2025-2-cs-43.verification: Swap non-conflicting adjacent operations in (B): W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), … → move W2(Y) before R1(X) (different items, no conflict) to get W2(X), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(Y), R1(X), W1(X) = serial $T_2, T_1$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-44.approach: Check each query against SQL semantics: a correlated subquery with EXISTS or COUNT(*) > 0 tests "this student has an enrolment in 1470", and a natural join on the only common column (rollno) pairs each student with their enrolments. SIZEOF is not an SQL function.
cse-2025-2-cs-44.given: Common columns: Students ∩ Enrolled = {rollno}; Courses is not used. Goal: names of students $s$ with some row (s.rollno, 1470, ·) in Enrolled.

steps.title: (A) EXISTS with a correlated subquery
steps.body: For each student $S$, the inner query returns the enrolment rows of that student in course 1470. `EXISTS` is true exactly when that set is non-empty, so $S$.name is output iff $S$ is enrolled in 1470. **Correct.**

steps.title: (B) SIZEOF is not SQL
steps.body: SQL has no `SIZEOF` function (it is a C operator). The query is syntactically invalid and returns nothing, so it is **not** a correct query.

steps.title: (C) COUNT(*) in a scalar subquery
steps.body: The subquery returns one number per student: how many enrolment rows it has in 1470. `0 < COUNT(*)` is the same condition as `EXISTS`, so (C) returns the same names. **Correct.**

steps.title: (D) NATURAL JOIN on rollno
steps.body: Students and Enrolled share only the column `rollno`, so `Students NATURAL JOIN Enrolled` pairs each student with each of their enrolments. Keeping rows with courseno $= 1470$ leaves exactly the enrolled students, and `S.name` projects their names. **Correct.** (A student enrolls in a course at most once, so no duplicate name per student; even with duplicates the set of names is right.)

optionAnalysis.reason: EXISTS on the correlated subquery is true exactly for students with an enrolment in 1470.
`SIZEOF` is not an SQL function, so the query is invalid.
`0 < COUNT(*)` of the correlated subquery is equivalent to EXISTS.
The natural join is on rollno (the only common column), and the WHERE keeps course 1470 enrolments.

cse-2025-2-cs-44.shortcut: EXISTS ≡ COUNT(*) > 0 for a correlated subquery; spot the non-SQL keyword (SIZEOF) and check the natural join's common columns.
pitfalls: Thinking a NATURAL JOIN also matches on other columns — here rollno is the only shared name (Courses is not in the join).
Accepting SIZEOF because it "looks right" — it is not part of SQL.
Confusing a correlated subquery with an uncorrelated one (the `E.rollno = S.rollno` condition is what makes it per-student).
cse-2025-2-cs-44.verification: Tiny instance: Students = {(1, Ann), (2, Bob)}, Enrolled = {(1, 1470), (2, 1500)}. (A), (C) and (D) all return {Ann}; (B) raises a syntax error ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-45.approach: Every access pays the L1 time; only L1 misses (10%) go to L2 and pay the L2→L1 penalty, and only those that also miss in L2 (20% of them) additionally pay the memory→L2 penalty. Nesting the penalties gives the AMAT in one line.
cse-2025-2-cs-45.given:
| Level | Time | Hit rate |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | 1 ns | 90% |
| L2 (penalty L2→L1) | 10 ns | 80% |
| Main memory (penalty → L2) | 100 ns | — |

steps.title: Who pays what
steps.body: Hierarchical access: every access first looks in L1 (1 ns). Of all accesses, $10\%$ miss L1 and are brought from L2 (10 ns). Of those, $20\%$ also miss L2 and must first be brought from main memory to L2 (100 ns). So the memory penalty applies to $0.1 \times 0.2 = 2\%$ of all accesses.

steps.title: Miss penalty of L1
steps.body:
An L1 miss is served from L2: it costs 10 ns, plus, when L2 also misses (probability $0.2$), the 100 ns transfer from memory:

$$\text{Penalty}_{L1} = 10 + 0.2 \times 100 = 10 + 20 = 30\ \text{ns}$$

steps.title: Average memory access time
steps.body:
$$\text{AMAT} = t_{L1} + m_{L1} \times \text{Penalty}_{L1} = 1 + 0.1 \times 30 = 1 + 3 = 4\ \text{ns}$$

Rounded to one decimal place: **4.0 ns**.

cse-2025-2-cs-45.shortcut: $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.1\,(10 + 0.2 \times 100) = 4$ — write the penalties nested, innermost first.
pitfalls: Using the global L2 miss rate as $0.2$ without multiplying by the L1 miss rate $0.1$ (the memory penalty applies to only $0.1 \times 0.2 = 2\%$ of accesses).
Weighting the L1 time by the hit rate only ($0.9 \times 1$): the L1 lookup is paid on every access in the hierarchical model.
cse-2025-2-cs-45.verification: Expand by outcome: 90% hit in L1 cost 1 ns; 8% hit in L2 cost $1 + 10 = 11$ ns; 2% go to memory cost $1 + 10 + 100 = 111$ ns. $0.9 + 0.88 + 2.22 = 4.0$ ns ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-46.approach: In a synchronous pipeline every stage takes one clock, so the clock period is the slowest stage plus the latch delay. $n$ instructions on a $k$-stage pipeline finish in $(k + n - 1)$ cycles.

steps.title: Clock period
steps.body:
The clock must accommodate the slowest stage and the latch:

$$t_p = \max(180, 250, 150, 170, 250) + 10 = 250 + 10 = 260\ \text{ns}$$

scene.caption: Slowest stage 250 ns + latch 10 ns = 260 ns per cycle

steps.title: Cycles for 1000 instructions
steps.body:
The first instruction needs $k = 5$ cycles; each of the remaining $999$ completes one cycle later:

$$k + n - 1 = 5 + 1000 - 1 = 1004\ \text{cycles}$$

steps.title: Total time
steps.body:
$$T = 1004 \times 260\ \text{ns} = 261{,}040\ \text{ns} = 261.04\ \mu\text{s}$$

This lies in the official range 260.20 to 261.20.

pitfalls: Summing the stage delays ($1000$ ns) as the cycle time — that is the non-pipelined time per instruction.
Forgetting the latch: $1004 \times 250 = 251$ µs.
Using $n \times k$ cycles instead of $k + n - 1$.
cse-2025-2-cs-46.verification: Steady state alone gives $1000 \times 260$ ns $= 260$ µs; the fill adds $4 \times 260 = 1040$ ns $\approx 1.04$ µs, total $261.04$ µs ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-47.approach: Insert 23 into leaf C: C overflows and splits, copying the new leaf's smallest key up into B; B then has 5 keys and splits, pushing its middle key up into A. Read off the new parent of the leaf holding $25^*$.

steps.title: Locate the leaf
steps.body: $23 < 49$ ⇒ from $A$ follow the first pointer to $B$. In $B$, $19 \le 23 < 33$ ⇒ follow the pointer between 19 and 33 to leaf $C$, which is full.

steps.title: Split leaf C and copy 23 up
steps.body:
C would hold $20, 22, 23, 25, 26$ (5 keys > 4). Split into $(20^*, 22^*)$ and the new leaf $(23^*, 25^*, 26^*)$; the new leaf's smallest key **23 is copied up** into $B$:

$$B = (7, 19, 23, 33, 44)$$

5 keys — $B$ overflows too.

scene.caption: Leaf split: 23 copied up — B now has 5 keys

steps.title: Split B and push 23 up
steps.body:
An internal split keeps two keys on each side and **moves** the middle key up: $(7, 19)\ |\ 23\ |\ (33, 44)$. Root $A$ becomes $(23, 49, 77, 83)$ — 4 keys, no further split.

The leaf $(23^*, 25^*, 26^*)$ holds keys in $[23, 33)$, so it hangs from the first pointer of the new right node $(33, 44)$.

scene.caption: Parent of the leaf with 25* is (33, 44)

steps.title: Read the answer
steps.body:
Parent of the leaf containing $25^*$ is $(33, 44)$; its smallest key is **33**.

The other leaf-split convention, $(20^*, 22^*, 23^*)\ |\ (25^*, 26^*)$, copies 25 up; $B = (7, 19, 25, 33, 44)$ then pushes 25 up and the leaf $(25^*, 26^*)$ again hangs under $(33, 44)$. Same answer.

answer.value: Smallest key in the parent $(33, 44)$ is **33**

cse-2025-2-cs-47.shortcut: Both C and B are full, so both split. B's middle key (the copied-up 23 or 25) goes to the root, and the leaf with 25 lands under B's right half $(33, 44)$.
pitfalls: Copying the middle key up from an internal split (internal splits move it; only leaf splits copy).
Answering 23: 23 moves up to the root and is no longer in the parent.
Forgetting that B overflows and answering from $(7, 19, 23, 33, 44)$, i.e. 7.
cse-2025-2-cs-47.verification: Search 25 in the new tree: root $(23, 49, 77, 83)$: $23 \le 25 < 49$ ⇒ second child $(33, 44)$; $25 < 33$ ⇒ first leaf $(23^*, 25^*, 26^*)$ ✓, and every node has ≤ 4 keys ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-48.approach: The page offset takes $\log_2 4096 = 12$ bits. An inner page table occupies exactly one page, so it holds $4096 / 8 = 512$ entries ⇒ 9 index bits. The outer index gets the remaining bits.
cse-2025-2-cs-48.given: Logical address $= 32$ bits, page $= 4096 = 2^{12}$ B, inner PTE $= 8$ B, page tables are one page in size.

steps.title: Inner page table index
steps.body:
One page of the inner table holds

$$\frac{4096}{8} = \frac{2^{12}}{2^3} = 2^9 = 512\ \text{entries}$$

so the offset within the inner page table page needs **9 bits**.

steps.title: Outer index
steps.body:
$$b = 32 - 9 - 12 = 11$$

The outer page table then has $2^{11}$ entries.

pitfalls: Using 4-byte entries out of habit (gives 10 inner bits and $b = 10$).
Splitting the 20-bit page number evenly (10 + 10) instead of fitting the inner table into one page.
cse-2025-2-cs-48.verification: Mapped size: $2^{11}$ outer entries × $2^9$ inner entries × $2^{12}$ B pages $= 2^{32}$ B ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-49.approach: someAlgo is the classic double-BFS: in a tree, a vertex farthest from any start vertex is an end of a longest path, so the second BFS returns the **diameter** of the tree. Run both BFS passes on the figure (vertices labelled A–N for reference).
cse-2025-2-cs-49.given: Tree of the figure, labelled A–N (labels added only for the explanation): edges A–B, B–C, B–E, D–E, E–F, F–G, E–H, H–I, H–J, H–K, K–L, K–M, M–N.

steps.title: First BFS from any vertex, say H
steps.body:
Distances from $v = H$: level 1 = E, I, J, K; level 2 = B, D, F, L, M; level 3 = A, C, G, N.

Maximum distance 3, reached by A, C, G and N. Take $u = N$ (any of them works).

scene.caption: BFS from v = H: farthest vertices at distance 3

steps.title: Second BFS from u = N
steps.body:
Distances from $N$: M 1, K 2, H 3, L 3, E 4, I 4, J 4, B 5, D 5, F 5, A 6, C 6, G 6.

The maximum is **6** (at A, C or G); output $d(u, z) = 6$.

scene.caption: BFS from u = N: maximum distance 6

steps.title: This is the diameter
steps.body: A longest path is G–F–E–H–K–M–N with 6 edges. No path is longer: every path between the two sides of E uses at most 2 edges on the left (to A, C or G) and at most 4 on the right (to N), giving $2 + 4 = 6$; paths not through E are shorter (e.g. N to I is 4). The double BFS returns the diameter whatever $v$ and tie-breaks are chosen (from $u = A$ the second BFS also reaches N at distance 6).

cse-2025-2-cs-49.shortcut: Recognise double-BFS = tree diameter, then just find the longest leaf-to-leaf path: two hops left of the hub E plus four hops to the far-right leaf, $2 + 4 = 6$.
pitfalls: Counting vertices on the path (7) instead of edges (6).
Stopping after the first BFS (its maximum, 3 from H, is the eccentricity of H, not the diameter).
cse-2025-2-cs-49.verification: Repeat with $v = A$: farthest is N at distance 6; BFS from N gives 6 again ✓. 14 vertices and 13 edges confirm the figure is a tree.

cse-2025-2-cs-50.approach: A DFA only needs to remember $prod(x) \bmod 7$. Since no symbol is a multiple of 7, the product is never 0, so the reachable values are exactly the 6 non-zero residues; multiplication by a fixed residue is a bijection, so all 6 are pairwise distinguishable.
cse-2025-2-cs-50.given: $\Sigma = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, state $r = prod(x) \bmod 7$, start $r = 1$, accept $r = 2$. Transition $\delta(r, s) = r \cdot s \bmod 7$.

steps.title: States are residues; 0 never occurs
steps.body: 7 is prime and every symbol is in $\{1, \dots, 4\}$, so a product of such numbers is never divisible by 7: residue 0 (and a dead state) never appears. Candidate states: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$.

steps.title: Transition table and reachability
steps.body: All six residues are reachable from the start state 1: $1, 2, 3, 4$ by one symbol, $5$ by "34" ($12 \bmod 7 = 5$), $6$ by "23" ($6$). The full table $\delta(r, s) = rs \bmod 7$ is on the canvas.

steps.title: All six states are distinguishable
steps.body:
Take states $r \ne r'$. Choose a string $w$ with $prod(w) \equiv 2 r^{-1} \pmod 7$ (every residue $1$–$6$ is a product of symbols, as shown). Then from $r$ the product is $2$ (accept) and from $r'$ it is $2 r' r^{-1} \ne 2$ (reject). Example: states 1 and 4 — $w = 2$ gives $2$ (accept) vs $8 \bmod 7 = 1$ (reject).

So no two states merge: the minimum DFA has **6** states (accepting state: 2).

cse-2025-2-cs-50.shortcut: Mod-$p$ product automaton over symbols coprime to $p$: states = the $p - 1$ non-zero residues, all distinguishable ⇒ $7 - 1 = 6$.
pitfalls: Adding a state for residue 0 or a dead state (answer 7): 0 is unreachable and the DFA is already complete.
Thinking only residues 1–4 are reachable because the alphabet is $\{1,2,3,4\}$.
cse-2025-2-cs-50.verification: Each column of the table is a permutation of $\{1, \dots, 6\}$ (multiplication by a unit), so the DFA is a permutation automaton: its minimisation keeps every reachable state when exactly one state accepts ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-51.approach: Total cycles $= \sum (\text{CPI}_i \times N_i)$. Since execution time $=$ cycles $\times$ clock period, the clock period is time divided by total cycles.
cse-2025-2-cs-51.given:
| Type | CPI | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Branch | 2 | $2.25 \times 10^8$ |
| Load | 5 | $1.20 \times 10^8$ |
| Store | 4 | $1.65 \times 10^8$ |
| Arithmetic | 3 | $1.30 \times 10^8$ |

Time $= 6.3$ s; total $6.4 \times 10^8$ instructions.

steps.title: Cycles per instruction type
steps.body:
- Branch: $2 \times 2.25 = 4.50$
- Load: $5 \times 1.20 = 6.00$
- Store: $4 \times 1.65 = 6.60$
- Arithmetic: $3 \times 1.30 = 3.90$

(all $\times 10^8$ cycles). Check counts: $2.25 + 1.20 + 1.65 + 1.30 = 6.40$ ✓.

steps.title: Clock period
steps.body: $$t_{clk} = \frac{6.3\ \text{s}}{21 \times 10^8} = 0.3 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s} = 3 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s} = 3.0\ \text{ns}$$

pitfalls: Using the plain mean of the CPIs $(2+5+4+3)/4 = 3.5$ instead of the count-weighted CPI (gives 2.8 ns).
Dropping the $10^8$ when converting to nanoseconds.

cse-2025-2-cs-52.approach: Trace the pointer: a partially initialised array has its remaining elements set to 0, `&arr[0] + 1` points at `arr[1]`, and `(*ptr)++` changes the array element itself, which `arr[1]` later reads.

steps.title: Initialisation
steps.body: `int arr[5] = {30,50,10};` — the missing elements are zero-initialised: $arr = [30, 50, 10, 0, 0]$.

steps.title: ptr points at arr[1]; a = 50
steps.body: `&arr[0] + 1` advances by one `int`, so `ptr = &arr[1]`. Then `a = *ptr = 50`.

steps.title: (*ptr)++ modifies arr[1]
steps.body: The parentheses make `++` apply to the pointed-to value: $arr[1] = 50 + 1 = 51$. `a` keeps its copy, 50.

pitfalls: Reading `(*ptr)++` as `*ptr++` (which would move the pointer instead of incrementing the value).
Using 50 for `arr[1]` in the sum — it was incremented through the pointer (answer 110).
Thinking `a` changes too: it holds a copy of the value.
cse-2025-2-cs-52.verification: Values used: $a$ (copy before increment) $= 50$, `arr[1]` after increment $= 51$, `arr[2]` $= 10$; $50 + 51 + 10 = 111$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-53.approach: Compose the functions symbolically: $f(n) = g(2n) = 2n + 10$, so $g(f(n)) = 2n + 20$. The loop runs for $n = 1, 2$.

steps.title: n = 2, then the loop stops
steps.body:
$f(2) = g(4) = 14$, $g(14) = 24$. $sum = 22 + 24 = 46$.

Then $n = 3$ fails $n < 3$, and the program prints **46**.

pitfalls: Running the loop for $n = 1, 2, 3$ (gives $46 + 26 = 72$).
Applying $g$ only once (forgetting the outer $g$): $12 + 14 = 26$.

cse-2025-2-cs-54.approach: Two monic quadratics are equal iff their root multisets are equal, so $\{\alpha, \beta\} = \{\alpha^2, \beta^2\}$. Either each root is fixed by squaring, or squaring swaps the two roots. List the distinct polynomials and count those with equal roots.
concepts: Equality of polynomials ⇔ equal root multisets

steps.title: Case 1: α² = α and β² = β
steps.body: $\alpha^2 = \alpha \Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha \in \{0, 1\}$, same for $\beta$. Polynomials (roots as multisets): $\{0, 0\}$, $\{0, 1\}$, $\{1, 1\}$, i.e. $x^2$, $x(x-1)$, $(x-1)^2$.

steps.title: Case 2: α² = β and β² = α
steps.body:
Then $\alpha = \beta^2 = \alpha^4 \Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha^3 - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha \in \{0, 1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ with $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$, and $\beta = \alpha^2$:

- $\alpha = 0 \Rightarrow \{0, 0\}$ and $\alpha = 1 \Rightarrow \{1, 1\}$ (already counted)
- $\alpha = \omega \Rightarrow \beta = \omega^2$, and $\alpha = \omega^2 \Rightarrow \beta = \omega^4 = \omega$: the same polynomial $(x - \omega)(x - \omega^2) = x^2 + x + 1$. **New.**

steps.title: Count and divide
steps.body:
Square invariant polynomials: $x^2$, $x^2 - x$, $(x-1)^2$, $x^2 + x + 1$ — **4** in total. Equal roots: $x^2$ and $(x-1)^2$ — **2**.

$$P = \frac{2}{4} = 0.5$$

cse-2025-2-cs-54.shortcut: Squaring must permute the roots: fixed points $\{0, 1\}$ give 3 multisets, a 2-cycle needs $\alpha^3 = 1$, $\alpha \ne 1$ ⇒ $\{\omega, \omega^2\}$. $2$ of $4$ have equal roots.
pitfalls: Counting ordered pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ instead of polynomials: $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ are the same polynomial, as are $(\omega, \omega^2)$ and $(\omega^2, \omega)$.
Missing the swap case and answering $2/3 \approx 0.7$.
cse-2025-2-cs-54.verification: Check $x^2 + x + 1$: roots $\omega, \omega^2$; squares $\omega^2, \omega^4 = \omega$ — the same set ✓. Check $x(x-1)$: squares of $0, 1$ are $0, 1$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-55.approach: Let the cut be $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. If $U < 0.4$ the piece containing 0.4 is $(U, 1)$ of length $1 - U$; if $U > 0.4$ it is $(0, U)$ of length $U$. Integrate the length against the density 1.
concepts: Expectation of a function of a random variable

steps.title: Length as a function of the cut U
steps.body:
$$\ell(U) = \begin{cases} 1 - U, & 0 < U < 0.4 \\ U, & 0.4 < U < 1 \end{cases}$$

($U = 0.4$ exactly has probability 0.)

steps.title: Add
steps.body:
$$E[\ell] = 0.32 + 0.42 = 0.74$$

This lies in the official range 0.70 to 0.80.

pitfalls: Answering 0.5 (the expected length of a fixed piece, e.g. the left one) — the piece containing 0.4 is more likely to be the longer one.
Swapping the cases: for $U < 0.4$ the point is in the right piece $(U, 1)$.
cse-2025-2-cs-55.verification: General formula: $\int_0^p (1-u)\,du + \int_p^1 u\,du = p - \tfrac{p^2}{2} + \tfrac{1 - p^2}{2} = \tfrac12 + p - p^2$; at $p = 0.4$: $0.5 + 0.4 - 0.16 = 0.74$ ✓. At $p = 0.5$ it gives the known $0.75$.
